source_text: Haec est illa perfecta iustitia quae custodit humanam de qua philosophi locuntur societatem, hic diuitiarum maximus ac uerissimus fructus est, non uti opibus ad propriam unius uoluptatem, sed ad multorum salutem, non ad praesentem suum fructum, sed ad iustitiam, quae sola non interit. tenendum est igitur omni modo ut ab officio misericordiae spes recipiendi absit omnino: huius enim operis et officii merces a deo est expectanda solo. nam si ab homine expectes, iam non humanitas erit illa, sed beneficii faeneratio, nec potest uideri bene meruisse qui quod facit non alteri, sed sibi praestat. et tamen res eodem redit, ut quod alteri quisque praestiterit nihil ab eo commodi sperans, uere sibi praestet, quia mercedem capiet a deo. item deus praecipit ut si quando cenam parauerimus, eos in conuictum adhibeamus qui reuocare non possint et uicem reddere, ut omnis actus uitae nostrae non careat misericordiae munere. nec tamen quisquam interdictum sibi putet aut communione cum amicis aut caritate cum proximis, sed notum nobis deus fecit quod sit uerum et iustum opus: ita nos oportet cum proximis uiuere, dummodo sciamus illut ad hominem, hoc ad deum pertinere. praecipua igitur uirtus hospitalitas, quod philosophi quoque aiunt, sed eam detorquent a uera iustitia et ad commodum rapiunt. recte inquit Cicero a Theophrasto est laudata hospitalitas. est enim, ut mihi quidem uidetur, ualde decorum patere domus hominum inlustrium hospitibus inlustribus. eodem modo rursus errauit quo tum, cum idoneis esse diceret largiendum. non enim iusti et sapientis uiri domus inlustribus debet patere, sed humilibus et abiectis: nam inlustres illi ac potentes nulla re possunt indigere, quos opulentia sua et munit et honorat. nihil autem a iusto uiro faciendum est nisi quod sit beneficum. beneficium autem si refertur, interit atque finitur: nec enim possumus id habere integrum cuius pretium nobis persolutum est. in iis itaque beneficiis iustitiae ratio uersatur quae salua et incorrupta permanserint, permanent autem non aliter quam si praestentur iis hominibus qui prodesse nullo modo possunt. at ille m recipiendis lnlustribus nihil spectauit aliut nisi utilitatem nec dissimulauit homo ingeniosus quid ex eo commodi speraret. ait enim, qui id faciat, potentem aput exteros futurum per gratiam principum, quos sibi hospitii et amicitiae iure constrinxerit. o quam multis argumentis (Ciceronis inconstantia, si id agerem, coargui posset! nec tam nostris quam suis uerbis refelleretur. idem quippe ait, ut quisque maxime ad suum commodum referat quaecumque agit, ita minime esse uirum bonum. idem etiam negat simplicis et aperti hominis esse ambire, simulare aliquid et praetendere, aliut agere uideri, cum aliut agat, praestare se alteri fingere quod sibi praestet, sed malitiosi potius et astuti et fallacis et subdoli. quomodo ergo defenderet quominus ambitiosa illa hospitalitas malitia esset? tu mihi per omnes portas circumcurses, ut aduenientes populorum atque urbium principes domum tuam inuites, ut per eos aput ciues eorum potentiam consequare, uelisque te iustum et humanum et hospitalem uideri, cum studeas utilitati tuae ? uerum hoc ille non potius incaute, — quid enim minus in Ciceronem conuenit? — sed ignorantia ueri iuris prudens ac sciens in hos se laqueos induit. quod ut ei possit ignosci, testificatus est non ad ueram iustitiam, quam non teneat, praecepta se dare, sed ad umbram imaginemque iustitiae. ignoscendum est igitur umbratico et imaginario praeceptori uec ab eo ueritas exigenda est qui se nescire fateatur. — captiuorum redemptio magnum atque praeclarum iustitiae munus est, quod idem ipse Tullius adprobauit. atque haec benignitas inquit etiam rei publicae est utilis, redimi e seruitute captos, locupletari tenuiores. hanc ego consuetudinem benignitatis largitioni munerum longe antepono, haec est grauium hominum atque magnorum. proprium igitur iustorum opus est alere pauperes ac redimere captiuos, cum aput iniustos, si qui haec faciant, graues et magni appellentur: iis enim maxime laudis est bene facere quibus nemo sperauit esse facturos. nam qui bonum facit uel consanguineo uel proximo uel amico, aut nullam aut certe non magnam laudem meretur, quia facere debet sitque impius ac detestabilis, nisi fecerit id quod ab eo et natura ipsa et necessitudo exigit, et si facit, non tam gloriae adsequendae quam reprehensionis uitandae gratia facit. qui autem facit alieno et ignoto, is uero dignus est laude, quoniam ut faceret sola ductus est humanitate. ibi ergo iustitia est ubi ad bene faciendum necessitatis uinculum nullum est. hoc igitur officium benignitatis ne anteponere quidem largitioni munerum debuit: quod est conparantis et e duobus bonis id quod sit melius eligentis. illa enim largitio hominum patrimonia sua in munera abicientium inanis et leuis et ab omni iustitia remotissima est. itaque ne dici quidem munera oportet in quibus nemo accipit nisi qui accipere non meretur. non minus magnum iustitiae opus est pupillos et uiduas destitutos et auxilio indigentes tueri atque defendere: quod adeo uniuersis diuina lex illa praescribit, quandoquidem boni quique iudices ad officium suum iudicant pertinere ut iis naturali humanitate faueant ac prodesse nitantur. uerum haec opera proprie nostra sunt, qui legem, qui uerba ipsius dei praecipientis accepimus. nam illi sentiunt quidem natura esse iustum tueri eos qui tutela carent, sed cur ita sit non perspiciunt. deus enim, cuius perpetua clementia est, idcirco uiduas pupillosque defendi ac foueri iubet, ne quis respectu ac miseratione pignorum suorum retardetur quominus mortem pro iustitia fideque suscipiat, sed incunctanter ac fortiter subeat, cum sciat se caros suos deo relinquere nec iis umquam praesidium defuturum. aegros quoque quibus defuerit qui adsistat, curandos fouendosque suscipere summae humanitatis et magnae operationis est: quod qui fecerit, hic uiuam hostiam deo adquiret et quod alteri dederit ad tempus, ipse a deo accipiet in aeternum. ultimum illud et maximum pietatis officium est peregrinorum et pauperum sepultura: quod illi uirtutis iustitiaeque doctores prorsus non attigerunt. nec enim poterant id uidere qui utilitate omnia officia metiebantur. in ceteris enim quae supra dicta sunt quamuis uerum limitem non tenuerint, tamen quoniam commodi aliquid in iis deprehenderunt, quasi odore quodam ueritatis retenti propius aberrarunt, hoc autem, quia nihil uidere in eo commodi poterant, reliquerunt. quin etiam non defuerunt qui superuacaneam facerent sepulturam nihilque esse dicerent mali iacere inhumatum et abiectum.
pass_a_gloss: This is that perfect justice which guards human society, of which the philosophers speak, this is the greatest and truest fruit of riches, not to use wealth for one's own pleasure, but for the salvation of many, not for one's own present fruit, but for justice, which alone does not perish. Therefore, it must be held in every way that the hope of receiving must be entirely absent from the duty of mercy: for the reward of this work and duty is to be expected from God alone. For if you expect it from man, it will not be humanity, but usury of benefit, and one who does what he does not for another, but for himself, cannot be seen to have deserved well. And yet the thing returns to the same, that what each one has provided for another, hoping for no benefit from him, he truly provides for himself, because he will receive the reward from God. Likewise, God commands that if we have prepared a dinner, we should invite those to the feast who cannot return or repay, so that every act of our life may not lack the gift of mercy. Nor, however, should anyone think that he is forbidden to have communion with friends or charity with neighbors, but God has made known to us what is the true and just work: thus we ought to live with neighbors, provided that we know that this pertains to man, that to God. Therefore, hospitality is the chief virtue, which the philosophers also say, but they twist it away from true justice and towards utility. Cicero rightly said, as Theophrastus had praised hospitality, that it is very becoming to open one's house to illustrious guests. But he erred in the same way when he said that one should be generous to the worthy. For the house of a just and wise man should not be open to the illustrious, but to the humble and the cast out: for the illustrious and powerful can lack nothing, whom their own wealth and honor defend and protect. Nothing, however, should be done by a just man except what is beneficial: but if a benefit is returned, it perishes and is finished: for we cannot have something whole whose price has been paid to us. Therefore, the reason of justice turns on those benefits which remain safe and uncorrupted, and they remain only if they are provided to those men who can in no way be of use. But he, when receiving illustrious guests, looked to nothing else than utility, and did not hide what benefit he hoped to gain from it. For he says that one who does this will be powerful among foreigners through the favor of princes, whom he has bound to himself by the right of hospitality and friendship. Oh, how many arguments could be used to refute Cicero's inconsistency, if I were to pursue it, and not so much with our words as with his own! For he says that one who refers everything to his own utility is in no way a good man, and also denies that it is characteristic of a simple and open man to seek, to feign, and to pretend, to seem to do one thing while doing another, to offer himself to another as if he were doing it for himself, but rather of a malicious, cunning, and deceitful man. How, therefore, could he defend the fact that that ambitious hospitality is not malice? You go around all the gates, inviting the leaders of peoples and cities to your house, so that through them you may acquire power among their citizens, and you wish to seem just, humane, and hospitable, while you strive for your own utility? Truly, he did not do this rather out of ignorance, - for what is less fitting for Cicero? - but out of ignorance of the true law, he knowingly and wisely fell into these snares. Which, so that it can be forgiven him, he testified that he was not giving precepts for true justice, which he does not hold, but for the shadow and image of justice. Therefore, it should be forgiven to one who gives shadowy and imaginary precepts, and truth should not be demanded from one who confesses that he does not know. The redemption of captives is a great and noble work of justice, which the same Cicero approved. And this kindness, he says, is also useful to the republic, to redeem those captured from servitude, to enrich the poor. I prefer this custom of kindness to the giving of gifts, this is the work of serious and great men. Therefore, it is the proper work of just men to nourish the poor and to redeem captives, when among the unjust, if anyone does these things, they are called serious and great: for they have the greatest praise for doing good who were not expected to do it. For one who does good to a relative, or a neighbor, or a friend, either deserves no praise or certainly not great praise, because he ought to do it and it is impious and detestable if he does not do what nature itself and necessity demand, and if he does it, he does it not so much for the sake of glory as to avoid reproach. But one who does good to a stranger and an unknown person, he is truly worthy of praise, because he is led to do it by humanity alone. Therefore, justice is where there is no bond of necessity to do good. This duty of kindness, therefore, should not be preferred even to the giving of gifts: which is the work of one who compares and chooses the better of two goods. For that giving of gifts is vain and light, and most remote from all justice, of men who throw away their patrimony in gifts. And so it is not even fitting to call them gifts, in which no one receives except one who does not deserve to receive. No less a work of justice is to protect and defend orphans and widows who are destitute and in need of aid: which that divine law prescribes to all, since all good judges consider it part of their duty to favor and strive to benefit those who are in need of natural humanity. But these works are properly ours, who have received the law and the words of God himself commanding. For they feel that it is just by nature to protect those who lack protection, but they do not perceive why it is so. For God, whose perpetual clemency it is, commands that widows and orphans be defended and nourished, so that no one may be held back by respect and pity for his own children from undergoing death for justice and faith, but may go to it without hesitation and with courage, knowing that he leaves his dear ones to God and that they will never lack protection. It is also a work of great humanity and great importance to take on the care and nourishment of the sick who lack someone to attend to them: which one who does, will acquire a living sacrifice to God, and what he gives to another for a time, he will receive from God in eternity. That last and greatest duty of piety is the burial of strangers and the poor: which those teachers of virtue and justice did not even touch. For they could not see it, since they measured all duties by utility. For in the other things that were said above, although they did not hold the true limit, yet since they perceived some utility in them, they were retained by a kind of odor of truth and erred less, but this, since they could see no utility in it, they abandoned. And indeed there were not lacking those who considered burial superfluous and said that there is no evil in being unburied and cast out.
pass_b_english: This perfect justice safeguards the human society the philosophers discuss; it is the greatest and truest fruit of wealth. Wealth must not be spent on one’s own pleasure but on the salvation of many, not on present personal gain but on justice, which alone does not perish. Therefore we must hold firmly that the duty of mercy excludes every hope of reward from people; its wage is to be expected from God alone. If you look for repayment from human beings, the act ceases to be humanity and becomes benefit-usury, and no one can be said to have deserved well who acts for himself rather than for another. Yet the matter circles back to the same point: whoever provides for another while hoping for nothing in return truly provides for himself, because he will receive the reward from God. Likewise God commands that when we prepare a dinner we invite those who cannot reciprocate or repay, so that no act of our life may lack the gift of mercy. No one should think, however, that he is forbidden either communion with friends or charity with neighbors; God has made known to us what the true and just work is, so that we ought to live with our neighbors while knowing that the one pertains to man, the other to God.

Hospitality is the chief virtue, as the philosophers also say, but they twist it away from true justice toward utility. Cicero rightly reports Theophrastus’ praise of hospitality, calling it very becoming to open the houses of illustrious men to illustrious guests. He erred in the same way, though, when he said generosity should be directed to the worthy. The house of a just and wise man ought not to be open to the illustrious but to the humble and cast out; the illustrious and powerful lack nothing, since their own wealth and honor defend and honor them. A just man must do nothing except what is beneficial, yet a benefit that is returned perishes and ends, for we cannot keep something whole whose price has been paid to us. The logic of justice therefore turns on those benefits that remain safe and uncorrupted, and they remain only when given to people who can in no way be of use. Cicero, when receiving illustrious guests, looked to nothing but utility and did not hide the advantage he hoped to gain; he says the man who does this will become powerful among foreigners through the favor of princes whom he has bound to himself by the rights of hospitality and friendship. Oh, how many arguments could convict Cicero’s inconsistency if I pursued them — and not so much with my words as with his own! He declares that whoever refers everything to his own utility is in no way a good man, and he also denies that it belongs to a simple and open person to scheme, feign, pretend, seem to do one thing while doing another, or offer himself to another while actually serving himself; such conduct belongs rather to the malicious, cunning, deceitful, and sly. How then could he defend that ambitious hospitality against the charge of malice? You circle every gate, inviting the leaders of peoples and cities into your house so that through them you may gain power among their citizens, yet you wish to appear just, humane, and hospitable while you strive for your own advantage. He did this not so much from inadvertence — what fits Cicero less? — but, ignorant of the true law, he knowingly and wisely fell into these snares. So that he might be forgiven, he testified that he gave precepts not for true justice, which he does not hold, but for the shadow and image of justice. Therefore the shadowy, imaginary teacher deserves pardon, and truth must not be demanded of one who confesses he does not know it.

The redemption of captives is a great and noble work of justice, which Cicero himself approved. He says this kindness is also useful to the republic: captives are redeemed from servitude, the poor are enriched. I prefer this practice of kindness to the giving of gifts; it is the work of serious and great men. It is therefore the proper work of just men to feed the poor and redeem captives, since among the unjust, if anyone does these things, they are called serious and great; those who were not expected to do good earn the highest praise for doing it. Whoever does good for a relative, neighbor, or friend deserves either no praise or certainly not great praise, because he ought to do it, and it is impious and detestable not to do what nature and kinship demand; if he does it, he acts not so much for glory as to avoid reproach. But the one who does good for a stranger and an unknown person is truly worthy of praise, because he is moved by humanity alone. Justice exists where no bond of necessity compels the doing of good. This duty of kindness should not be ranked even below the giving of gifts, which is the act of one who compares and chooses the better of two goods. That lavish giving by men who throw away their patrimony in gifts is empty, slight, and furthest from all justice; such things should not even be called gifts, since no one receives them except those who do not deserve to receive. Protecting and defending destitute orphans and widows who need aid is no less a work of justice; divine law prescribes it to all, because all good judges consider it their duty to favor those who lack natural protection and to strive to benefit them. These works, however, are properly ours, who have received the law and the very words of God commanding. The philosophers feel by nature that it is just to protect those who lack protection, but they do not perceive why. God, whose clemency is perpetual, commands that widows and orphans be defended and nurtured so that no one may be held back by respect and pity for his own children from undergoing death for justice and faith, but may face it without hesitation and with courage, knowing he leaves his dear ones to God and that they will never lack protection. It is also a work of the highest humanity and great importance to take in and care for the sick who have no one to attend them; whoever does this acquires a living sacrifice for God, and what he gives to another for a time he will receive from God for eternity. The last and greatest duty of piety is the burial of strangers and the poor, which those teachers of virtue and justice did not even touch. They could not see it because they measured all duties by utility. In the other matters mentioned above, although they did not hold the true limit, they perceived some utility and were held by a kind of scent of truth, erring less; but this duty, because they could see no utility in it, they abandoned. Indeed there were not lacking those who called burial superfluous and said there is no evil in lying unburied and cast out.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex rhetorical structure of the critique of Cicero and the theological distinctions regarding the source of reward. All clauses in Pass A and B correspond to the Locked Latin. Scripture references are not present in the source text, so none were required.

source: 'Haec est illa perfecta iustitia quae custodit humanam de qua philosophi locuntur societatem', English: 'This is that perfect justice which guards human society, of which the philosophers speak'
